Subjects

Islamic law

Sharia, fiqh, legal theory and their modern interpretation.

This section collects what modern authors say about fiqh and its sources: how the schools worked, what happened to Islamic law under colonial rule and state codification, and whether it can be revived, reformed or has to be rethought. Wael Hallaq argues that the modern state cannot house the sharia at all. Tariq Ramadan and Khaled Abou El Fadl argue for reform from within the tradition, and Yusuf al-Qaradawi and Taqi Usmani write as practising jurists answering questions of finance, family and worship.

Fatwa collections and manuals are here too, but most of those entries point to free copies hosted elsewhere.

Where to begin

A reading order, earliest first. Each title opens the text or the free copy.

  1. 1891 · Book
    Sirat al-Nu'man ↗ Shiblī Nuʿmānī

    A biography of Abu Hanifa, and a nineteenth-century Indian view of what a school of law is for.

  2. 2001 · Book
    Authority, Continuity, and Change in Islamic Law ↗ Wael Hallaq

    How legal authority worked in the classical schools, and how it was reshaped later.

  3. 2001 · Book
    Speaking in God's Name: Islamic Law, Authority and Women ↗ Khaled Abou El Fadl

    Examines who speaks for God in legal opinions, and when authority becomes authoritarianism.

  4. 2006 · Book
    Sexual Ethics and Islam: Feminist Reflections on Qur'an, Hadith, and Jurisprudence ↗ Kecia Ali

    A study of the legal tradition on sexual ethics, read by a historian and a feminist.

  5. 2009 · Book
    Radical Reform: Islamic Ethics and Liberation ↗ Tariq Ramadan

    Argues for a reform of Islamic legal method that starts from ethics.

  6. 2013 · Book
    The Impossible State: Islam, Politics, and Modernity's Moral Predicament Wael Hallaq

    Hallaq's case that the modern state and the sharia cannot be combined.
